item.title: Chinese nationals accused of smuggling synthetic drugs into US prisons on drug-soaked paper
item.description: Two Chinese nationals allegedly shipped synthetic opioids and cannabinoids to U.S. co-defendants who soaked paper in the drugs and mailed them to inmates.
item.content:encoded:
Two Chinese nationals were arrested in China after allegedly supplying synthetic drugs that prosecutors say were imported into the United States and later distributed to inmates at federal and state prisons nationwide.

Lisa Xing, 36, and Zhanwen Song, 38, were charged in a superseding federal indictment in the Eastern District of Texas with drug trafficking and money laundering offenses tied to an alleged scheme that supplied synthetic opioids, cannabinoids and other drugs from China for distribution in U.S. correctional facilities.

FBI Director Kash Patel touted the case in a post on X, writing that the defendants allegedly trafficked "dangerous synthetic drugs from China into the United States — including smuggling them into our prison systems."

"This FBI and our Homeland Security Task Force partners will keep finding and disrupting these networks wherever they operate," Patel wrote. "Great work by @FBIDallas and our law enforcement partners."

EXCLUSIVE: FENTANYL DEATHS PLUNGE 22% AS TRUMP WHITE HOUSE TOUTS CRACKDOWN ON DEADLY DRUG CRISIS

According to prosecutors, Xing and Song shipped synthetic drugs to co-defendants Adell Willis of Texas and Judy Ly of Michigan, who allegedly dissolved the drugs into liquid, soaked sheets of paper in the mixture and mailed them to inmates in federal and state prisons across the country.

Willis and Ly were indicted in May on charges including conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

FEDERAL INMATES MAY SOON GET TABLETS WITH MESSAGING CAPABILITIES AS BUREAU OF PRISONS MAKES MODERNIZATION PUSH

"The indictment alleges that a China-based supplier and a domestic distributor worked together to bring deadly synthetic drugs into the United States for distribution across the country," U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs said.

The Justice Department said China's Ministry of Public Security arrested Xing, Song and 19 additional alleged co-conspirators, seized 475 kilograms of synthetic cannabinoids and shut down four illicit manufacturing sites. Officials said the investigation was coordinated through an FBI-Chinese Ministry of Public Security counternarcotics working group established earlier this year.

If convicted, each defendant faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years in prison and up to life behind bars.

item.title: Local GOP leader slams $50K taxpayer 'slush fund' for families of detained, deported immigrant breadwinners
item.description: A Virginia GOP leader calls Arlington County's $50,000 in taxpayer-funded grants for families of deported illegal immigrants a "slush fund."
item.content:encoded:
A Virginia GOP leader is pushing back against a new county program to provide taxpayer-funded grants to the families of illegal immigrants whose primary wage earner was detained or deported by federal immigration authorities.

Arlington County, which sits across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C., endorsed a plan on Sept. 2 to appropriate $50,000 for the social safety-net program. Under the terms of the project, the funds would be given to the nonprofit Arlington Thrive, which would provide up to $2,000 to the families to cover basic needs.

"This flies in the face of the Trump administration policy, and it is a detriment to taxpayers of Arlington – tens of thousands of whom are conservative and Republican and oppose this policy," Matthew Hurtt, chairman of the Arlington County GOP, told Fox News Digital.

'ALIEN HARBORING' ACCUSATIONS FLY AS DC-AREA COUNTY SPENDS TAXPAYER FUNDS TO BLUNT ICE

Hurtt described the money as a "slush fund" designed to further oppose the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration. He noted that since Arlington Thrive is a nonprofit, it is exempt from transparency protocols that normally apply to government agencies.

The County Board praised the program at a special meeting, where it voted 4-0 with one member absent.

FIRST ON FOX: ICE QUIETLY ARRESTS JAW DROPPING NUMBER OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS IN MASSIVE DC AREA OPERATION

"We stand with our immigrant families, and we will not stop doing so," Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said. "We are valuing the families of those that have been displaced and removed."

The move follows a recent law enforcement operation in which more than 1,300 illegal immigrants were arrested over a two-week period in the Washington, D.C., and Virginia area.

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

In January, as part of the county's opposition to immigration enforcement, de Ferranti urged residents to report sightings of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to county authorities.

Arlington County, as well as other counties in Northern Virginia, have for years tried to subvert the Trump administration's efforts to fight illegal immigration through various sanctuary policies, Hurtt said.

DOJ ACCUSES MARYLAND OF 'ACTIVE AND DELIBERATE EFFORT' TO PREVENT DEPORTATIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS: LAWSUIT

"Arlington County, Fairfax County, and other Northern Virginia counties are completely run by far-left activists who love this kind of program," he said. "They have, for years, since President Trump's first administration, sought to be the first line of defense against the orange man."

"So if something happens in Washington that is supported by Republicans, the county board in Arlington and Fairfax does exactly the opposite," he added.

Meanwhile, Hurtt said, county leaders have pushed for voters to support bond measures for critical services, which are covered by additional taxes.

"Every single election cycle, the Arlington County board puts hundreds of millions of dollars on the ballot in the form of bond issues for basic services — school improvements, road construction, and other projects that they deem necessary," he said.

"What that tells voters is that they aren't prioritizing those projects, projects that they bond out and borrow dollar after dollar, but they're prioritizing these far-left projects like a slush fund for illegal aliens," he added.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Arlington County Democrats and the County Board for comment.

item.title: Raiders star Brock Bowers shockingly undergoes meniscus trim surgery as fantasy managers fume ahead of Week 1
item.description: Las Vegas Raiders star Brock Bowers underwent meniscus surgery in Dallas and is expected to miss a game or two, blindsiding fantasy football managers.
item.content:encoded:
News from the Las Vegas Raiders has fantasy football managers across the country fuming, especially those who made sure to draft close to the start of the NFL season.

Star tight end Brock Bowers underwent a meniscus trim on Tuesday in Dallas, and he’s now expected to miss "a game or two," according to ESPN.

This is a tremendous blow to the Raiders’ new-look offense under head coach Klint Kubiak, as Bowers, who dealt with lingering knee issues last season, was expected to be Kirk Cousins’ top target entering the new campaign.

The report added that Bowers was banged up "a little in camp," and he had the injury diagnosed last week. Surgery was scheduled and Dr. Daniel Cooper operated on Bowers, who will now hope to return in Week 3, though the "game or two" timeline can always vary depending on the player.

While Bowers isn’t expected to miss significant time at the moment, an interesting part of the report is the fact the Raiders knew since last week, but it was never mentioned.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Of course, teams don’t care how fantasy football lineups are impacted throughout the season. But for a league that has roughly 40 million Americans playing fantasy football annually, which relies heavily on disclosed injuries in terms of drafting and lineups being placed, Bowers’ injury is shocking those who own him as the 2026 season kicks off in Seattle on Wednesday night.

Bowers is also a top draft choice for many in fantasy football considering the volume he receives for the Raiders as well as his outstanding rookie campaign, where he totaled 1,194 yards on 112 receptions with five touchdowns.

Had fantasy managers known about Bowers’ injury, skepticism about taking him with such a high pick would’ve likely entered the minds of many.

To make matters worse, Kubiak was asked during a press conference just hours before news broke about Bowers' injury if he and Maxx Crosby, who dealt with injuries last season and wasn't used much during preseason contests, would be available on Sunday.

"We’re expecting to have all our guys ready for Sunday," Kubiak replied.

So, either Kubiak was blatantly lying about Bowers' condition, or he didn't know that one of his best players could be missing time after getting surgery on Tuesday in Dallas. Not the best way to start off the new year.

Bowers was unable to see his rookie-year production in 2025 due to his PCL sprain and bone bruiser that pestered him since Week 1’s victory over the New England Patriots. He missed several weeks, ultimately playing in 12 games (eight starts) before being placed on the season-ending injured reserve for the final two weeks of the year.

As NFL reporter Ari Meirov pointed out on X, a meniscus trim usually takes four-to-six weeks to recover from, but the Raiders appear optimistic Bowers will be back before then. A full meniscus repair is a season-ending injury — Minnesota Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy missed his entire rookie campaign due to that exact injury.

In the meantime, fantasy managers could be quick to pick up Michael Mayer, the Raiders’ second tight end, off waivers if he’s available. Mayer was always going to work within this offense, as Bowers can be placed anywhere on the line of scrimmage due to his route-running abilities for a tight end.

Now, Cousins will need to rely on Mayer to pick up the slack against the Miami Dolphins, whom they host at Allegiant Stadium on Sunday.

item.title: U.S. Open door is wide open, and an American man must walk through it and win the title
item.description: Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe meet in the U.S. Open semifinals with Jannik Sinner, Carlos Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic all already eliminated.
item.content:encoded:
American men's tennis has run out of excuses.

World No. 1 Jannik Sinner withdrew from the U.S. Open prior to the tournament with a knee injury. Then, Novak Djokovic lost in the first round.

Finally, in a stunning upset, Ben Shelton sent defending champion Carlos Alcaraz home after a five-set battle that ended at 3:33 a.m. Wednesday morning.

BEN SHELTON TAKES DOWN CARLOS ALCARAZ TO EARN THE BIGGEST WIN OF HIS CAREER IN LATEST US OPEN MATCH EVER

Now Shelton and Frances Tiafoe will meet in the semifinals on Friday, which guarantees that an American man will play for the U.S. Open championship on Sunday afternoon in Flushing.

That's nice, but it isn't enough. One of them needs to hoist the trophy.

Andy Roddick remains the last American man to win a Grand Slam singles title. He did it at the U.S. Open in 2003, which means the drought is well into its third decade.

We've spent more than 20 years searching for the next guy. There have been promising teenagers, big servers, top-10 players and a lot of perfectly respectable runs to the second week of major tournaments. But this is America, and we don't do "respectable." We do dominant.

Taylor Fritz reached the U.S. Open final in 2024. Tiafoe made the semifinals in 2022. Shelton got there in 2023. Those are all good runs. But American men have been living off close calls for long enough, and it's time to finish the job. There's arguably never been a better opening for it to happen.

The two best men's tennis players in the world aren't standing in the way. Sinner, the No. 1 player in the world and reigning Wimbledon champion, withdrew before the tournament with a right knee injury.

Alcaraz, the reigning Australian Open and U.S. Open champ, made it to New York after missing the past two majors with a wrist injury, but Shelton beat him. Djokovic's 39-year-old body betrayed him in a stunning first-round loss to Mariano Navone.

Alexander Zverev is still alive, and he finally got over the Grand Slam hump at the French Open earlier this year, in part due to Alcaraz's absence. He's a serious threat, but he's not at the level of either Sinner or Alcaraz, the two players who had combined to win nine straight major titles before Zverev broke through in Paris.

The remaining field has good players. It doesn't have an unbeatable one, and sometimes in tennis that's all you can ask for.

Shelton certainly didn't get a free pass into the semifinals. Alcaraz entered their quarterfinal with a 13-0 record against American men in Grand Slam matches.

Shelton dropped the first set in a tiebreak, then ripped through the next two to take control of the match. Alcaraz answered with a dominant fourth set, and more than four hours after they started, it came down to a deciding tiebreak.

LADIES AT THE US OPEN WERE CAUGHT ON CAMERA TAKING NOTICE OF A SHIRTLESS CARLOS ALCARAZ

Despite facing the most pressure-packed moments of his career, Shelton came through to beat the 23-year-old Spaniard. Shelton has had plenty of near misses, which made this victory feel like a breakthrough.

The power has never been in doubt. His serve is a weapon, his athleticism jumps off the screen and he feeds off an enthusiastic crowd better than almost anyone on tour.

But could he beat one of the sport's giants when the match was on the line and the lights shone their brightest? Finally, that answer is a resounding yes.

Tiafoe had to answer a different question. He fell behind fellow American Alex Michelsen by two sets and a break in their quarterfinal and was staring at a quiet exit after squandering a golden opportunity.

Things looked especially bleak because Michelsen hadn't dropped a single set in the tournament up to that point.

Tiafoe could have folded, especially after all the years of people waiting for him to turn his talent into a major title. Instead, he fought his way back and won in a fifth-set tiebreak.

Tiafoe is 28. He's not old, but he's not the young prospect with unlimited time anymore. This is his third trip to a major semifinal, all at the U.S. Open. At some point, the breakthrough has to become more than making it to Friday night.

And Tiafoe knows it.

"We're going to enjoy this, but we got to keep going," he said after beating Michelsen.

Shelton is 23 and probably has more opportunities ahead of him. But ask Dan Marino how many more Super Bowl appearances he thought he'd have after he made his first one at 23. The answer was zero.

There will be plenty of talk about how great Friday's semifinal is for American tennis, and it is. Arthur Ashe Stadium will be packed and fired up to watch two American stars with big personalities, huge games and a real chance to end a 23-year major-title drought.

But the celebration can't peak in the semifinal.

We already know an American can reach the final. Fritz did it two years ago, then Sinner beat him in straight sets. Getting another man to the last Sunday would show consistency. Winning could change the sport in this country.

That may sound dramatic, but look around. American women's tennis has continued producing major champions. Coco Gauff, Madison Keys and Sofia Kenin have all won Grand Slam singles titles in this decade. The men keep giving fans encouraging signs and asking them to wait a little longer.

We can't wait much longer.

Whoever wins between Shelton and Tiafoe will have the New York crowd, a winnable final and the opportunity American men's tennis has spent 23 years trying to create. Sinner, Alcaraz and Djokovic are already gone. The last obstacle will be one very good player on one Sunday afternoon.

Many people probably want to already label this tournament as a success because an American man is guaranteed to at least make the final. I'm not one of them. At this point, it's victory or failure.

The door is open and it's time to finally walk through it.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy juror who backed the defense also publicly cheered Karen Read's acquittal
item.description: A juror in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial previously voiced support for Karen Read online. A mistrial was declared in Clancy's case after jurors could not reach a verdict.

item.title: Mel Gibson says 'monster' epic 'Passion' sequel spans spiritual realms — and this time, it's in English
item.description: Mel Gibson revealed why "The Resurrection of the Christ" ditches ancient languages for English and takes viewers on a spiritual journey across realms.
item.content:encoded:
Mel Gibson is ditching ancient languages for English in his upcoming two-part follow-up to "The Passion of the Christ," describing the new epic as a "trip" that will take moviegoers across spiritual realms.

Gibson spoke exclusively with Fox News contributor Raymond Arroyo about his upcoming two-part follow-up, "The Resurrection of the Christ," including his decision to use English in the new films. 

The interview comes as the original 2004 film returns to theaters for a special Fathom Events re-release.

The full interview is featured on the "Arroyo Grande Show with Raymond Arroyo" YouTube channel.

'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' WRITER REVEALS MEL GIBSON'S DARK SPIRITUAL WARNING ABOUT 'PASSION' FOLLOW-UP

"You had a focal point, and it was about human suffering," Gibson said of the original film. "That was a rather simpler message to get across, and I think the complexity of an event like the resurrection, which is impossible to comprehend really, one has to delve more into sources.

"I thought it was just silly to make people read subtitles in a foreign language when they were dealing with such heady concepts. So, it asks more of you, but we help them along with their own language."

"The Passion of the Christ" is a biblical drama depicting the crucifixion of Jesus Christ in excruciating detail. It starred Jim Caviezel as Jesus and focused on the final 12 hours of Jesus’ life, with dialogue mainly in Aramaic, Hebrew and Latin.

MEL GIBSON'S 'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' REVEALS FIRST PHOTOS AFTER LONG-AWAITED PASSION SEQUEL

"The Resurrection of the Christ: Part One" is set for release May 6, 2027, with Part Two scheduled for May 25, 2028. While the original film focused on the final hours of Jesus’ life, Gibson said the new films will explore the resurrection and the days that followed.

Gibson said the upcoming films take viewers on a "trip" into other realms and explore how humanity is connected to them. He said the films are meant to show viewers the "big picture."

"It takes a pretty broad trip [from] our own broken world to, you know, other realms and stuff with different natures, and connects all of them, I hope — because we're all connected, and we all know we're connected," he said.

NEW BOOK ON ARCHAEOLOGICAL EVIDENCE FOR JESUS ROCKETS TO TOP OF BESTSELLER LIST

Gibson said the writing and pre-production process has taken more than a decade, and the new films are arriving over 20 years after the original premiered. He suggested the timing may be for a reason, saying, "There’s no accidents anywhere."

"I thought I was late. It was just too late, 23 years later, but it's probably just right. It's not my timing," Gibson said.

When asked whether he considers the project his own "resurrection" as a filmmaker, Gibson described the undertaking as a transformative, communal journey.

MEL GIBSON REVEALS ‘THE PASSION OF THE CHRIST’S’ MOST SURPRISING LEGACY IN NEW RAYMOND ARROYO INTERVIEW

"It’s a monster. It’s a massive undertaking," Gibson said. "I think, how can one not be changed by just being involved in that? And I didn't do it alone, either. There was a lot of people that came with me. So, it's a journey, right? That was a communal experience."

item.title: Minnesota Vikings surprisingly demote former first-round pick JJ McCarthy to third string
item.description: J.J. McCarthy dropped to third string as Carson Wentz was named backup behind starter Kyler Murray for the Vikings' Week 1 matchup vs. the Packers.
item.content:encoded:
J.J. McCarthy was once supposed to be "the guy" for the Minnesota Vikings. But going into Week 1 of the 2026 NFL regular season, he's not even the guy's backup.

That's because Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell named Carson Wentz the team's backup quarterback for Sunday's home game against the Green Bay Packers.

And on Aug. 11, O’Connell named Kyler Murray the starter for Sunday’s game and the foreseeable future.

VIKINGS QB BATTLE MEETS EXPECTED END AS KYLER MURRAY STARTS OVER MCCARTHY

O’Connell told reporters Wentz would serve as the backup, and the team later released its depth chart, listing McCarthy behind him. Wentz was deemed more prepared to step in if Murray cannot play.

"I'm looking at that right now as a week-to-week thing," O'Connell said. "Carson, he's got almost 100 career starts. What he was able to do last year from the standpoint of very limited repetitions but being able to apply a career's worth of experience, that's kind of what you need to do as a backup quarterback — especially early on when so much of the emphasis is going to be on getting Kyler as comfortable as we can possibly get him.

"But J.J. is still going to get a bunch of great work..."

McCarthy's work will be mostly running some of the scout team for the Vikings, particularly during weeks they face a more mobile quarterback.

And that is a mighty fall for McCarthy, who was drafted in 2024 with expectations he would eventually be the team's franchise quarterback.

This announcement is merely the latest in a series of setbacks McCarthy has faced since the Vikings selected him No. 10 overall in the 2024 NFL Draft.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

You’ll recall that the Vikings traded up to select McCarthy, passing on Bo Nix, who has since become Denver’s starter.

But McCarthy never played as a rookie after suffering a season-ending torn meniscus in his right knee during the Vikings’ first preseason game against the Raiders. That injury cost him an entire developmental year and left the team relying on Sam Darnold during a playoff season.

McCarthy finally became Minnesota’s starter in 2025, opening with an impressive fourth-quarter comeback at Chicago and earning NFC Offensive Player of the Week honors.

But then things went sideways.

McCarthy struggled with turnovers and more injuries, including a concussion, and finished the season with 11 TD passes and 12 interceptions.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

The offseason also dealt McCarthy a blow because the Vikings didn't sit tight and bank on him developing into a good quarterback. They went out and found his replacement by adding Murray.

And this: If Murray plays well this year, as some believe he will, McCarthy may never get a chance to be the starter for the Vikings.

That’s because Murray will be a free agent after the season, and the Vikings aren’t about to repeat their Sam Darnold mistake. Darnold, you’ll recall, played well in 2024, but the Vikings didn’t re-sign him for 2025 and beyond despite his strong performance.

Darnold won the Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks last year.

The Vikings thus would likely re-sign Murray if he plays well.

And that would leave McCarthy a backup player for the rest of his time with the team, regardless of how rosy O'Connell paints things.

"I'm really excited to get a chance to continue to work with him," the coach said. "Want to make it week-to-week so when we need to declare something different, we can and we will. This gives us the best chance to win this Sunday."

item.title: Top Republican names who he says is really leading Democrats — and it's not Schumer or Jeffries
item.description: Top Senate Republican Rick Scott claims Chuck Schumer isn't leading Democrats — saying AOC, Zohran Mamdani and Hassan Piker call the shots.
item.content:encoded:
DALLAS — A top Senate Republican warned that the real leaders of the Democratic Party aren’t the top two Democrats in Congress.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., weren’t the ones calling the shots for Democrats — it’s the far-left progressives, both inside and out of Congress, that are leading the way.

"Let's be clear, the leader of the Democrat Party is not Schumer, it's not Jeffries," Scott said. "It's Hasan Piker, it is AOC and [Zohran] Mamdani."

REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG

Republicans are congregating in Dallas, Texas, to pitch why they should maintain power in Congress and energize their base during a midterm cycle in which Democrats are fighting to retake control of both chambers.

Scott, who once led the Senate GOP’s campaign arm known as the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), argued that Schumer and Senate Democrats could "salivate all they want, but their message is horrible."

That message is driven by the likes of streamer Hasan Piker, who has come under fire from both Republicans and Democrats, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION

"They're going to say, ‘Gosh, we want men to play in women's sports, to destroy women's sport,’" Scott said. "They can talk about socialism, how they want to kill all the capitalists."

"I tell people, you go vote for a Democrat, which is now a socialist, right? Then you better buy a bunch of guns," he continued. "Because you can vote socialism in, ask the people in Venezuela, but guess what? You can't get rid of it without guns."

Still, Republicans are facing political headwinds as November creeps closer, with the Iran war still raging, prices at the gas pump and checkout line still high, and a fresh trade war with Canada putting GOP incumbents and candidates in a bind.

'WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?': ONE CRUCIAL TRUMP DECISION IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN

And midterm elections are more often than not a referendum against the party in power. Scott, however, believes that Republicans are going to "actually have a good cycle," and maintain control of the Senate.

"The reason is we have a better message and we have great candidates," Scott said. "If you look at our Senate candidates, I mean, how would you like to be out and defend [Abdul] El-Sayed's record of being antisemitic and hating this country."

Much of the purpose of the convention, Scott acknowledged, was to remind voters that while his name isn’t explicitly on the ballot, the midterm elections were all about President Donald Trump.

Trump is set to speak on Wednesday night as the NFL starts again, and as Republicans formulate their final message to their base. And that message is that if Democrats win, Trump’s agenda will stall completely.

"There's no question the Trump agenda is on the ballot," Scott said. "If you want the Trump agenda accomplished, we have to control the House, we have to control the Senate."

"And if the Democrats control the House, they're gonna impeach him for combing his hair the wrong way," he continued. "So we've gotta control the House and we gotta control the Senate."

item.title: Florida woman accused of DUI crashes SUV into parked car, then makes bizarre plea to police caught on camera
item.description: Surveillance video allegedly shows a Florida woman smashing into a parked car in Daytona Beach before she pleaded with police officers not to take her to jail.
item.content:encoded:
A Florida woman accused of plowing an SUV into a parked car appeared to downplay the collision before making a personal plea to officers investigating her, newly released video shows.

"I thought we were all friends," 24-year-old Elizabeth Boucher told Daytona Beach police during the Aug. 30 encounter.

Surveillance video released by police shows an SUV smashing into a parked Honda with enough force to shove it across a front lawn and out of the camera’s view.

But when an officer asked Boucher what happened, she offered a far less dramatic account caught on police bodycam video.

BODYCAM SHOWS NANTUCKET OFFICIAL SLURRING, SWAYING DURING DUI STOP AFTER CRASHING INTO SIGN: POLICE

"I guess I hit the front light of those cars, but I don’t know what really happened," Boucher said.

"You didn’t just hit the front of the car," the officer fired back. "You just took the car completely off."

Body camera video shows the officer then asking Boucher for her driver’s license. She instead hands him a passport.

BODYCAM VIDEO SHOWS CANADIAN WOMAN ALLEGEDLY GIVING FALSE NAME BEFORE DEPUTIES DISCOVERED 12 FAKE IDS

"That’s a passport," he tells her before again asking for her license.

As the roadside investigation unfolded, Boucher pleaded with officers not to lock her up.

"It’s just a vape. I know. It didn’t even work," she said. "Please don’t take me to jail over this."

An officer later told Boucher the case had been shifted from a civil crash investigation to a criminal DUI investigation and read her Miranda rights.

Asked whether she would perform field sobriety exercises, Boucher refused, according to the video. She also declined a breath test after an officer formally requested one.

REPEAT DRUNKEN-DRIVING OFFENDER ACCUSED OF KILLING HONORS COLLEGE STUDENT HEADING HOME FROM WEDDING

When Boucher again invoked their supposed friendship, an officer responded, "But we still have a job to do."

"I know. I’m not resisting arrest," Boucher said. "I just want to make sure my daughter gets what she needs."

An officer then instructed her to lean against a vehicle "so you don’t fall."

"Am I going to jail?" Boucher asked moments later.

"Yes," the officer replied.

The woman whose vehicle was struck also told officers that Boucher had confronted and slapped her after the crash, according to the bodycam video.

SUSPECTED DRUNK DRIVER KILLS 2 PEDESTRIANS IN VIOLENT CHAIN-REACTION CRASH ON MANHATTAN'S UPPER WEST SIDE

"Did she touch you at any point?" an officer asked.

"Yeah, she smacked me right here," the woman alleges before saying she wanted to press charges.

After she was placed under arrest, Boucher appeared confused by the slow-moving process.

"Why am I sitting here all alone? Why is nothing happening?" she asked.

"That’s normally what happens when you are arrested," an officer told her.

Boucher was charged with driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, DUI involving damage to property or another person, refusing to submit to DUI testing, battery by touching or striking, resisting an officer without violence and possessing a controlled substance without a prescription, according to police.

An attorney for Boucher could not immediately be identified.

She was released from jail Aug. 31 and has pleaded not guilty to the charges, according to court records. 

She is expected back in court in October.

item.title: Florida sues Netflix, alleges streamer tracked children after promising families privacy
item.description: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier alleges Netflix secretly harvested children's behavioral data to build the ad business it vowed never to create.
item.content:encoded:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued Netflix on Wednesday, accusing the streaming giant of misleading subscribers by promising an ad-free, privacy-focused service while secretly collecting years of behavioral data — including from children's profiles — to build the advertising business it long insisted it would never create.

The 66-page lawsuit alleges Netflix built its brand by assuring consumers that paying a monthly subscription meant they could avoid the surveillance-driven advertising model used by other major technology companies. Instead, Florida alleges Netflix quietly collected extensive user data before launching its ad-supported platform in November 2022.

"Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape Big Tech surveillance. That was false," Uthmeier said in a news release announcing the lawsuit. "Netflix collected detailed data on children and families, designed its product to keep kids watching, and then commercialized that information to launch the advertising business it promised never to build. Parents, not corporate executives, direct the upbringing of their children. Netflix should expect to be held accountable."

The complaint points to repeated public statements from Netflix executives who touted the company as different from advertising-supported competitors. Among them, the lawsuit cites former CEO Reed Hastings, who said during a 2020 earnings call that Netflix was "not integrating everybody's data," adding, "We don't collect anything," and describing the streaming service as "the safe respite" from companies that exploit users through advertising.

WASHINGTON POST FACES CLASS-ACTION LAWSUIT ALLEGING 'SURVEILLANCE PRICING' OF SUBSCRIBERS

Florida alleges those assurances were misleading because Netflix built what the lawsuit describes as a massive behavioral-data operation that records how subscribers use the platform. According to the complaint, Netflix tracks billions of user interactions, including what subscribers watch, search for, pause, rewind, skip and abandon, along with information about their devices and locations. The state alleges Netflix uses that information to improve its recommendation systems and support its advertising business.

The lawsuit places particular emphasis on Netflix's Kids Profiles, which the company markets as dedicated spaces designed for children. Florida alleges Netflix encouraged parents to create children's profiles by describing them as "Great for kids" and a child's "own space" while continuing to collect and analyze children's viewing behavior through the same telemetry systems used for adult accounts.

PARENTS PUSH CONGRESS TO ACT ON KIDS' ONLINE SAFETY AFTER JURIES FIND META AND YOUTUBE LIABLE FOR HARM

Florida also accuses Netflix of using so-called "dark patterns" to keep viewers engaged. The complaint alleges autoplay, which is enabled by default on Kids Profiles, is intentionally designed to extend viewing sessions, increase binge watching and generate additional behavioral data, particularly from children.

The state further alleges Netflix expanded into the advertising business it once rejected by allowing advertisers and advertising technology companies to use subscriber data for audience targeting and campaign measurement after launching its ad-supported tier in November 2022.

The lawsuit accuses Netflix of violating the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act and the Florida Digital Bill of Rights. Among other claims, Florida alleges Netflix unlawfully shared sensitive personal data collected from children without obtaining the consent required under state law.

MARYLAND MOVES TO BAN SURVEILLANCE PRICING IN GROCERY STORES

Uthmeier is asking the court to permanently block the alleged practices, order Netflix to delete data the state says was deceptively collected from Floridians, stop using historical subscriber data to support its advertising business, purge behavioral data collected through Kids Profiles, prohibit the use of alleged dark-pattern designs and impose civil penalties authorized under Florida law.

Netflix did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: Fans are going crazy for a viral $38 French dip sandwich that is taking over the US Open
item.description: Salt Hank's $38 French dip sandwich has US Open fans waiting in half-hour lines for prime rib, provolone, caramelized onions, and au jus dip.
item.content:encoded:
Few experiences are as universal as paying an obscene amount of money for food and drinks at a sporting event. I mean, did you even go to a game if you didn't pony up north of $20 for a hot dog and a Pepsi Zero Sugar?

Perhaps it's due to widespread cases of the munchies, but fans at the US Open understand this is how it is, and in fact they're embracing it, with huge lines of folks forming for the privilege of scarfing down a $38 sandwich.

But before you say, "I'd never spend that on a sandwich at the US Open," quit lying to yourself.

$100 HOT DOGS GET OVER-THE-TOP TREATMENT WITH CAVIAR, WAGYU AND 24-KARAT GOLD

The sandwich is the work of a joint in the West Village called Salt Hank's, and they've got people waiting in half-hour lines for their French dip sandwich, which features prime rib, provolone cheese, caramelized onions, and horseradish aioli served with a side of shoestring fries and a nice little sidecar of au jus to dunk it in.

Salt Hank's is selling an insane amount of these sandwiches, despite the price tag.

And you know what? I get it and would absolutely buy one as well.

When I first heard about this, I was one of those who was saying there'd be no way I'd drop that much on a sandwich.

Then I heard it was a French dip, and I changed my tune.

I think the French dip might have the highest batting average of any sandwich I've ever had. I can't think of a bad one. I've had bad subs, bad Cuban sandwiches, bad cheesesteaks, and even an occasional "meh" Italian beef.

But the French dip? It always brings it.

The only thing I don't like is having to eat it in a US Open environment. The French dip is a sitting sandwich. It's not a stand against a wall or balance on your thighs while sitting in a stadium seat sandwich.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

This is because au jus is a fickle, non-viscous mistress. One wrong move and it's everywhere.

You'd inevitably go to take a bite, and some influencer laying down a TikTok dance would bump into you, splashing beef stains all over your Lacoste polo you pulled out of the back of your closet because, well, tennis.

I mean, at the price, they should do you a solid and throw in a Tide To Go pen.

But from what I've been seeing, the sandwich is good enough that people are not just overlooking the potential laundry nightmares but also the substantial whack to the ol' bank account.

item.title: Ukraine strikes deep into Russia’s Arctic gas heartland as Trump pushes Putin toward peace
item.description: Ukrainian drones struck Novy Urengoy, sparking a fire in Russia's top natural-gas region roughly 1,740 miles from Ukraine's border in the Arctic.
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian drones struck deep into Russia’s Arctic north Wednesday, sparking a fire at an industrial facility in Novy Urengoy, a city in the heart of Russia’s most important natural-gas producing region, according to Russian officials and the Associated Press.

Regional Gov. Dmitry Artyukhov said Russian air defenses repelled the attack but falling drone debris caused a fire at an industrial site. He did not identify the facility, and the extent of the damage was still being assessed, Reuters reported Wednesday.

Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point appeared to claim involvement, posting: "Guess who covered more than 3,300 km and successfully hit the target."

The extraordinary strike comes as Washington makes a renewed push to end the more than four-year war even as Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range attacks on each other.

UKRAINE UNLEASHES MORE THAN 400 DRONES NEAR MOSCOW IN ONE OF WAR'S BIGGEST ATTACKS

Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, President Donald Trump said he had just spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin and suggested both Moscow and Kyiv may be prepared to negotiate.

"We had a great conversation. He is wanting to make a deal. And if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that would be very nice," Trump said.

Asked what was holding up an agreement, Trump pointed to the personal animosity between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling them "two people that hate each other."

"These are two people that are tired of fighting," Trump added.

Trump’s comments followed a weekend diplomatic push by U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who traveled to Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to revive negotiations. The talks produced no breakthrough, according to the Associated Press.

RUSSIAN STRIKES CONTINUE FOLLOWING VISIT BY WITKOFF AND KUSHNER TO KYIV

Russia resumed major missile and drone attacks on Kyiv shortly after the American delegation left Ukraine, killing five people and wounding 35 on Tuesday, Reuters reported.

A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that the simultaneous diplomacy and military escalation reflects a long-standing dilemma for Western governments trying to engage Moscow.

"You have to talk, you have to explain," the source said, arguing that communication is necessary to prevent misunderstandings.

RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY

But the source said Russian officials can interpret Western outreach differently.

"Whenever you talk with them, they consider that this is a Western weakness," the source said, adding that the assessment was based in part on informal contacts with Russian officials.

The source also said Putin’s recent emphasis on Russian "military progress in Ukraine" appeared aimed in part at Washington, projecting strength as U.S. officials seek to revive negotiations.

The escalation is taking an increasing toll on civilians. The United Nations said last month that Russian attacks killed or wounded more Ukrainian civilians in July than in any month since March 2022, with 437 killed and more than 2,600 wounded.

More than 16,800 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and more than 51,000 wounded since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians and says its strikes are aimed at military and military-related facilities.

DRONE OFFENSIVE HITS RUSSIAN OIL TANKERS AND REFINERIES AT 'INDUSTRIAL SCALE' AS MOSCOW BANS DIESEL EXPORTS

United24 described Wednesday’s attack as the deepest Ukrainian drone strike inside Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Novy Urengoy lies roughly 1,740 miles from Ukraine’s border. Artem Zhoga, Putin’s envoy to Russia’s Urals Federal District, said a Ukrainian drone had attempted to strike a fuel-and-energy facility in Yamal, according to Meduza.

The city sits in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, the country’s dominant natural-gas producing region. About 80% of Russia’s natural gas is extracted there, according to Interfax data cited by the Associated Press.

Artyukhov said there were no reported casualties.

The attack was part of a broader Ukrainian drone assault on Russia. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces also struck targets around the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, including a naval base, an oil-loading terminal, military port facilities and warships capable of carrying cruise missiles, according to the Associated Press.

Russian authorities said four people, including a child, were killed and 29 wounded in the Novorossiysk attack.

Russia, meanwhile, continued its own long-range campaign against Ukraine Wednesday. Russian drones struck the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, killing two civilians and wounding three, while another wave of attacks on Kyiv killed one person and wounded 14, according to Reuters.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Rick Springfield says he killed a man while entertaining troops during Vietnam War

item.title: Rubio designates Ecuadorian gang linked to drug trafficking a terrorist group
item.description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the designation during a visit to Quito, accusing Los Tiguerones of aiding cartels and attacking civilians, police and journalists.
item.content:encoded:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday said he has designated a new Ecuador-based gang as a foreign terrorist organization and specially designated global terrorist.

Los Tiguerones, which has been linked to narcotrafficking and other illicit activity, has been accused of funding criminal activity against law enforcement and civilians.

"Los Tiguerones is yet another Ecuadorian gang helping Mexican cartels move and export illicit drugs to fund terrorism and criminal activity including attacks against civilians, law enforcement, and journalists," Rubio said in a post on X.

Rubio added that the group was also behind the notorious 2024 attack on an Ecuadorian television station, when armed men stormed the studio and took staff hostage during a live broadcast.

ARMED GUNMEN TAKE OVER ECUADOR TV STUDIO DURING LIVE BROADCAST, THREATEN STAFF: 'A TERRORIST ACT'

During the raid, attackers forced staff to the floor at gunpoint and allegedly stuffed a stick of dynamite into an employee’s pocket, according to The Associated Press (AP). The assault unfolded on live television for 15 minutes before the feed was cut, the AP reported. At least 13 suspects were reportedly arrested after police regained control of the building.

Rubio said Wednesday’s decision comes on the heels of the designation of three other groups, including Los Lobos and Los Choneros, in July.

"They're not ordinary. These are violent, bloodthirsty terrorist organizations. And we have to make sure that we continue to pursue them," Rubio said. 

The announcement was made while Rubio was visiting Quito, Ecuador, as part of a three-nation tour to strengthen economic and security ties with Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.

TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT

During a press conference, Rubio said the U.S. will also target corrupt officials accused of collaborating with terrorists as part of efforts to dismantle the organizations.

"We'll be announcing the designation of seven former members of the government here, officials for accepting bribes and for betraying their most essential duties," he said.

The designation will cut such terrorist groups off from U.S. financial assets, property and other resources that could be used to carry out attacks.

item.title: Ted Cruz battles 'The View' on Clarence Thomas and affirmative action, as host says 'Welcome to being Black'
item.description: Ted Cruz defended Clarence Thomas' affirmative action stance on "The View," sparking a heated exchange with Sunny Hostin and Whoopi Goldberg.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, defended Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas' affirmative action stance on Wednesday as he faced questioning from the co-hosts of "The View" about his new book.

"Clarence Thomas, he stated that affirmative action diminishes achievements because it allowed people to believe he had not earned his place at Yale and I think we can all agree that affirmative action was put in place to provide opportunities to qualified Black students, like Thomas, because those institutions historically would not give them the opportunities to go," co-host Sunny Hostin said during the interview about Cruz's new book, "The Incomparable Clarence Thomas."

"So what I don’t understand how you handle in the book is, why is the lesson from his experience that we should eliminate the remedy rather than eliminate the racism that made the remedy necessary? I don’t understand that," Hostin asked Cruz.

Thomas sided with the 6-3 majority ruling in 2023 on affirmative action, saying the court's decision "sees the universities’ admissions policies for what they are: rudderless, race-based preferences designed to ensure a particular racial mix in their entering classes."

JUSTICE THOMAS RECALLS WHY HE WASN'T FRIENDS WITH ALITO IN LAW SCHOOL: 'CLARENCE, YOU WERE SCARY'

Hostin said, "I mean, I genuinely don't understand the framing in the book about that."

Cruz said that affirmative action "encompasses a lot of things" before describing Thomas' viewpoint.

"If you're talking about removing barriers, if you're talking about expanding access, then I'm for that, he's for that, everyone is for that. If you're talking about quotas and discriminating based on race, then Justice Thomas has been the clearest defender of the principle that the Constitution prohibits the government discriminating based on race," he began, before Hostin questioned why the justice felt his Yale degree was "diminished because people felt that it was a result of affirmative action."

'LOOK AT ME!' JUSTICE FIRES BACK AT CRITICS WHO DARE QUESTION HIS BLACKNESS

Cruz responded, "So there was a reason for that. When he came out of Yale Law School, he had done very well in law school. He applied. Not a single law firm would hire him. Every law firm he interviewed said, ‘No.'"

"Welcome to being Black," co-host Whoopi Goldberg interjected.

Goldberg pointed to Thomas being a constitutional scholar before asking Cruz, "How does he not remember that we weren't part of the Constitution? Right? We were not. So there's a reason people didn't start off, we weren't all equal."

TED CRUZ SHUTS DOWN TRUMP SUPREME COURT TALK WITH A FIERY 'NOT JUST NO, BUT HELL NO'

Cruz argued that Thomas talked about that at length, saying, "Look, the Civil War and Reconstruction, the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments. The 13th Amendment ended slavery. The 14th Amendment protected equal protection. And the 15th Amendment protected the right to vote, specifically for African Americans."

"So why are we still talking about it if it protects all of this? That's the thing I guess," Goldberg said before ending the interview as the show ran out of time.

Cruz's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Earlier in the show, Goldberg admonished "The View" audience after they groaned upon announcing Cruz would be a guest later in the show.

"Look, this is a place where Barbara Walters made sure that anybody who wanted to come and have a good conversation could come," she said, shutting down the booing. "So we want people to come, and we want to engage them. We don’t agree with them always. We don’t jell with them always, but we are respectful, and I know you will be too."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

She compared it to swallowing a burp and said, "Sometimes you know stuff, it’s like a burp. It comes up and so just swallow it back down."

item.title: Sophie Cunningham has a bikini boat day during the WNBA break, Sydney Sweeney's ad is a talker & replacing LSU
item.description: Sophie Cunningham hits the boat while the WNBA takes a break, and the Rams face an insane 15,000-mile travel schedule for their Melbourne opener.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

To the WNBA, NBA, NHL, MLB and FIFA ... rest easy, your watch has now ended.

The KING is back. The NFL season is upon us. Is it a little weird to be kicking off the new year on a Wednesday? Sure. No argument there.

But will we care at 8:20 tonight when AJ Brown gives us our first anytime touchdown cash of the betting season? Nope.

We will not.

AJ BROWN SAYS THERE'S BEEN SILENCE BETWEEN HIM AND EX-TEAMMATE JALEN HURTS SINCE HIS MOVE TO NEW ENGLAND

Welcome back, NFL. Goodness, we've missed you.

And, of course, welcome to a Hump Day Nightcaps — the one where Sophie Cunningham enjoys a day on the boat before taking in some opening night football action from Seattle.

What else? I've got a 49ers wife saying goodbye to summer before her husband kicks things off in Australia, a rundown of the Rams' INSANE travel schedule this week, and if the SEC were to expel LSU from the conference, who would YOU pick as a replacement?

It'll never happen (right?), but it's still a thinker. And in this class, we like to challenge ourselves!

Grab you some grilled chicken for National Grilled Chicken Day — throw it out and fry some WINGS like a man — and then settle in for a Hump Day 'Cap!

Look, I love the NFL. It's No. 1 for me, followed by college football and MLB. So, I'll never complain about a Wednesday night kickoff.

That being said ...

It is odd that the schedule-makers decided this was the best matchup possible. Did they watch the Super Bowl earlier this year? It stunk. It was never, ever close. Why on earth did they think we'd want to follow it up with ... the exact same matchup?

The Vrabel stuff from the offseason was a juicy storyline in March, but that's faded away (for now). I guess you could argue that AJ Brown makes it more interesting. But other than that? It's pretty much the same teams, minus Ken Walker.

Oh well. It's a nitpick, I know. I'm just happy football is back.

I'm also happy that Sophie Cunningham is getting some nice rest while the WNBA takes a month off for the FIBA World Cup over in Germany.

She deserves it.

She leads off today's class:

That's how you spend the finals day(s) of summer ... one last boat trip before the leaves start to fall and the WNBA playoffs kick into gear.

Sophie gets it. I know the girls are overseas right now playing in the world cup, but I'd rather be here, in the U-S-of-A, on a boat. Point to Sophie Cunningham!

PS: I had a reader bring this up a few days ago, and had to doublecheck it to be sure. Anyone here want to take a guess at when the FIBA championship game is?

This Sunday ... at 2 p.m.

The FIRST NFL Sunday of the year! Right at peak hours for RedZone. Amazing. They don't even stand a chance back here in the states.

OK, let's move it along because I have to fire up the Hard Rock app and see if I can get this NFL betting season started with a bang.

Or, you know, I guess I could try and use Novig for all my sports betting needs this season ...

Goodness gracious. I saw that ad making the rounds over on Elon's Twitter this morning, and thought it was AI. Seriously. I know Sydney Sweeney doesn't shy away from anything, but even I thought there was no way that was real.

It is real, and it's a TALKER.

"The campaign was about embracing a fun idea," Sweeney in a statement, according to Variety. "The concept is simple: cut through the noise and put the focus entirely on sports. The campaign brings that idea to life with confidence, humor and a playful edge."

Yep. The focus of that ad is certainly all on the sports! No argument here, Sydney.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Hump Day class into a big NFL night. First up? We've got Pats-Seahawks tonight, but did you know we have another game tomorrow?

Rams-49ers ... in Melbourne! It's on Netflix, which is dumb, but that's the world we now live in. It's also, technically, taking place on Friday since Australia is a billion hours ahead of us.

The Niners left the states for this game last week. The Rams? They left YESTERDAY:

"The Rams will spend more than 30 hours on an airplane, travel over 15,000 miles, cross 7 time zones, and play a football game, yet technically be back in Los Angeles less than 72 hours after leaving."

That's insane. Australia is 14 hours ahead of us, which means tomorrow night's game will actually be taking place on Friday at 10:35 a.m. in Melbourne.

And the Rams are going to have been there for a cup of coffee before strapping in and hitting the field.

No idea if it's gonna work, but I'm excited to see if it does!

Next? You know what's probably not gonna work? Kicking LSU out of the SEC. I just don't see it happening. I know the SEC has a big meeting this week about it, but come on. Let's be real for a second. That ain't happening.

If it DID, though, who would you want to replace the Tigers?

First of all ... "hobo on a ham sandwich" and "I've got rocks in my driveway that are smarter than that" are two absolute bangers from John Kennedy.

There is nobody better at their craft right now. He's the GOAT.

Secondly ... I think I'd go with: Miami, Va. Tech, FSU, or my wild card, Tulane. That's right.

Tulane!

Don't forget, Tulane was a founding member of the SEC and competed in the conference until 1966. The Green Wave have three SEC titles to their name. They're already in Louisiana, so you stay in the state.

They were also in the playoffs last year!

Not ridiculous, right?

... Right?!

OK, that's it for today. Good Hump Day, everyone. Welcome back, NFL.

And welcome back to 49ers LB Fred Warner's wife, Sydney! She's celebrating the return of football from a beach in Hawaii as the offseason officially comes to a close.

See you tomorrow.

Who would you pick to replace LSU? Let me know! Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

item.title: Sharon Stone says she 'nearly died' after 'Basic Instinct' opened the door to Hollywood's dark side
item.description: Sharon Stone says "Basic Instinct" opened "dark doors" that attracted dangerous people into her life, nearly consuming her before light saved her.
item.content:encoded:
Sharon Stone is opening up about how she survived Hollywood's dark side after starring in her hit movie "Basic Instinct."

The actress became an international star after she played Catherine Tramell, a seductive crime novelist and alleged serial killer, in the 1992 erotic thriller. However, Stone recently shared that portraying Tramell took a psychological toll on her and drew dangerous people into her orbit.

During an appearance on the "Mayim Bialik's Breakdown" podcast this week, Stone spoke about times when she's gotten too close to dark characters she's played and "scared the living s--- out of myself." Bialik asked her for an example, and she replied, "When I did ‘Basic Instinct,’ and I had to really look at darkness, and yet I was very still young and inexperienced."

'TEACHER'S PET' STAR MAMIE VAN DOREN SAYS SHE FELT 'USED' AS YOUNG ACTRESS NAVIGATING HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE

She continued, "I didn't understand about holding the core, the core self, the golden self, and then wrapping the character around it with the power of the self driving it. But just bringing it all in there and looking at it all, I opened some dark doors, right?"

"And some of those dark doors really scared the living s--- out of me, because I saw some real, real darkness," Stone remembered. "And what happened then is that real dark people identified and came into my life thinking, 'Oh, you really are like me. You're like me.'"

"And so darkness came into my life. Dark people, dark things, dangerous things came into my life because they thought, 'You're like me.' And then people believed some of the dark things that were said about me because they thought, 'Oh, you couldn't do that if you weren't like that because you've mirrored me to me.'"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

While speaking with Bialik and her co-host, Jonathan Cohen, Stone said the experience taught her to be more discerning about what and whom she allowed into her life.

"Really the one thing you got to remember is just because the devil's a very interesting person at the cocktail party doesn't mean you should invite that person, give them a seat. Don't give that person a seat," she said.

The Emmy Award winner explained how she learned to protect herself from people drawn to darkness, emphasizing the importance of maintaining her "core self."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Don't ever give up the core," she said. "You can't be porous."

"You just can't be porous because if any of it gets in, all of a sudden the dark people, they want to be around you," Stone continued. "They want to come to you. They think, 'Oh, you're like me.' And when they find out that you're not like them, they get upset. They get very upset."

Stone recalled that at one point, she felt that the darkness almost consumed her. She credited her survival to the strength of her "core self" and anchoring herself in a higher spiritual frequency.

"When the darkness came, I nearly died," she said. "But the light saved me. The light is what saved me. And the universal consciousness of light that vibrated at my frequency is what saved me."

'BLIND SIDE' STAR QUINTON AARON SAYS HE 'SAW JESUS' WHILE IN A COMA AFTER NEAR-FATAL STROKE

"Fortunately, enough of me held to the light and that just the crack where it got in was dangerous," Stone added.

During her podcast appearance, Stone also revealed that she received a life-or-death spiritual message following her near-fatal stroke.

In September 2001, the "Casino" star suffered a massive, life-threatening stroke at the age of 43. Stone spent nine days in the hospital after a ruptured artery that caused a brain bleed, requiring emergency surgery to repair the vessel.

While speaking with Bialik and Cohen, Stone claimed she encountered five glowing entities of light in a surreal vision during the early days of her recovery.

"When I was first home from the hospital, I couldn’t sleep at night, and I was sleeping in the day," Stone remembered. "When I was laying on the couch, sleeping and awake, these orbs sort of presented themselves to me. These five orbs presented themselves to me and they sort of talked to me, but in a digital language."

She admitted that she had never previously spoken about the experience because she found it almost impossible to explain. Stone said that she believed the encounter carried a premonition that she would soon lose custody of her then one-year-old son Roan.

"I just kept saying to them, ‘I don’t know if I’m supposed to stay here or if I’m supposed to die,’" Stone recalled of her conversation with the orbs. "And they said, ‘You’re supposed to stay.’ And I said, ‘I can only stay if two of you will stay with my son. Because I don’t want him to be alone, and I think he’s gonna get taken from me.’"

"Sure enough, he was taken from me," she continued. "And I said, ‘We have to have an agreement. The two of you will stay with him and protect him.’ And they agreed. And they said, ‘But your destiny requires that we stay with you.’"

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Stone and her ex-husband Phil Bronstein adopted Roan in 2000. A year later, Bronstein filed for divorce, citing irreconcilable differences. The former couple shared custody of Roan after finalizing the divorce in 2004, though Bronstein became Roan’s primary caretaker. Stone later adopted sons Laird and Quinn, now both 20, as a single mother.

The actress has previously said she could not fully discuss the original custody decision because of a confidentiality agreement, but she has claimed her "Basic Instinct" image was used against her in court, saying a judge asked Roan whether he knew his mother made "sex movies."

After Bialik asked how long her experience with the orbs lasted, Stone replied, "Several days."

"Wow," Bialik said.

However, Stone told Bialik that she was not frightened by the encounter.

"I was curious," she said, "but very much at peace."

item.title: Skillet frontman John Cooper talks about the risks of talking politics and why he wants to 'stay in his lane'
item.description: John Cooper of Skillet explains why he avoids mid-concert political rants, referencing Bruce Springsteen and Aaron Lewis' critique of the music icon.
item.content:encoded:
We live at a time when it seems like everything is politicized and everyone is jonesing to make their opinion heard. That's all well and good, but probably not what you want to hear when you show up to a concert, as John Cooper, frontman of the rock band Skillet, pointed out during an appearance on OutKick's "Tomi Lahren is Fearless."

When you shell out some serious coin, do you really want to be lectured by a seventy-something musician who's rolling in money about the evils of Donald Trump?

Me neither, and count Cooper as one of the few entertainers who understands that.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Lahren asked the rocker about his openness when it comes to talking about faith and politics, and if there are risks involved in doing so.

"Yeah, definitely. I would say there's not as much of a risk if you're on the left because you will get praised by all of the powers that be," Cooper said. "Now, of course, you're still risking something — there's going to be some fans that don't like it, so I don't want to say they're not risking anything. That's actually not fair, but you will get opportunities from some of the institutional powers."

SKILLET'S JOHN COOPER SAYS WOKE ACTIVISTS HAVE 'BIG HEARTS' BUT ARE 'HURTING THEMSELVES'

But while he has no problem talking politics, he gets where people are coming from when they want entertainers to zip it on the political talk.

"I agree with people when they're like, I don't want to see some actor come up and yell at me about Iran or whatever they're on about; I don't even know if they even know what they're talking about, you know?"

It would seem Lahren knew precisely the type of person he was referring to.

"Yeah. Like the (Bruce) Springsteen of the world," she said.

The two agreed that Springsteen's penchant in recent years for going on mid-concert political diatribes is wearing a little thin.

"It just gets a little bit exhausting," Cooper said. He then pointed to a lyric in Staind frontman Aaron Lewis' 2021 song "Am I The Only One," in which he talks about how he "quits singin' along/Every time they play a Springsteen song?"

However, as Cooper noted, Springsteen's politics don't change the fact that he's an incredible songwriter. It just shows that artists have a choice when it comes to getting political or focusing on the music.

"The Boss is amazing," Cooper said. "One of the greatest songwriters, certainly, of (his) generation, and I still listen to him. But I'm like, 'I don't want people to feel that way about me.' I know some people do, but I'm trying to stay in my lane as best as I can."

item.title: Naomi Osaka 'doesn't give a f---' about US Open outfit hate, says her Haitian 'blood' makes her who she is
item.description: Naomi Osaka fired back at critics on Instagram Threads, comparing the backlash over her bold U.S. Open outfits to scrutiny of her mental health stance.
item.content:encoded:
Naomi Osaka claims she doesn't care about what her critics think of her or her extravagant outfits, but she cares enough to call them out on social media.

The four-time Grand Slam winner donned a number of different, very bold pre-match outfits throughout the U.S. Open, a trend she's set for many years at this point in her career. After being bounced from the tournament in the Round of 16, Osaka had clearly reached her limit of online criticism regarding her ensemble.

"You know…idgaf [I don’t give a f---] if you don’t like me. I don’t mind being the first to do something and getting trashed for it," Osaka wrote on Instagram Threads. "This happened when I talked about mental health and for some reason it’s happening with my clothes lol. I’m literally Haitian it’s in my blood to be this way, as long as the people after me have an easier path it’s worth it."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Osaka was born in Osaka, Japan, and plays under the Japanese flag, but her father, Leonard Francois, is from Jacmel, Haiti, hence her nod to her line about having Haitian blood. She and her family moved from Japan to Long Island, New York, when she was three years old.

Osaka kicked off her 2026 U.S. Open journey by wearing a short-sleeved hoodie, red and black arm sleeves, and a full-length skirt ahead of her first-round match. She also wore a red and black headband around her cornrow-style hair, and later explained that it was a tribute to NBA legend Allen Iverson.

HATERS OF FASHION ATTACK ARYNA SABALENKA WITH 'STREETWALKER' INSULT SIMPLY BECAUSE SHE WORE FISHNET AT US OPEN

Ahead of her fourth-round loss to Elena Rybakina, Osaka wore a lavish coat done by KidSuper and a headband with the NBA logo on it before ditching it for a visor during the match.

Osaka infamously wore an outfit she explained was inspired by a jellyfish in a children's book at the Australian Open.
